t: Introduction: why a commission examination is needed
n: In this lecture we talk about the commission forensic medical examination. In investigations and court hearings concerning improper performance of professional duties, questions arise that require special medical knowledge. In accordance with legislation, a commission forensic medical examination must be ordered in such cases. We shall therefore consider in turn the ordering, composition, conclusion and evaluation of this examination.

The regulatory basis of commission examination. The procedure for ordering and conducting it and evaluating the conclusion is laid down by the Law "On Forensic Examination" and by the Criminal Procedure and Civil Procedure Codes. In addition, there are special departmental rules for conducting commission examinations. That is, the examination is not conducted arbitrarily but within the framework of law and rules.

Grounds for ordering. The examination is ordered on the basis of a decision of an inquiry officer, investigator or prosecutor, or a ruling of the court. In the descriptive part of the document, the circumstances of the case are first set out, then the type of examination and to whom it is assigned. The operative part gives the questions that the commission of experts must resolve. Thus the ordering document has three links: the ground, the descriptive part and the operative part.

Questions put to the experts. The questions must be precise, clear and consistent with the aims of forensic examination. They must not go beyond the competence of the commission of forensic medical experts. This means that the commission answers questions within its special knowledge, not extraneous ones.

Materials submitted to the commission. The case materials, medical records and other objects necessary for the conclusion are submitted; they are listed in the decision. In exceptional cases, photocopies signed by the head of the institution and certified with a seal may be used. Remember: a commission examination based on separate extracts from a case history or on certificates is not permitted.

t: Additional documents when bringing to liability
n: When a person is being held liable, additional documents are also needed. The commission must be given the materials of earlier departmental and official inquiries, as well as references stating the employee's training, experience and category. In the event of death, the conclusion of the forensic medical examination of the corpse or the pathoanatomical record and additional laboratory results, for example histological and forensic chemical, are submitted. Missing materials may be requested by the head of the expert institution from the body that ordered the examination.

Impossibility of giving a conclusion. In three cases the commission cannot give a conclusion: if the question lies outside special knowledge, if the objects are unsuitable or insufficient, or if the state of science does not allow an answer. In such cases a reasoned document is drawn up. This document is sent to the body, that is, the person, who ordered the examination.

t: Where and by whom it is conducted
n: Where and by whom a commission examination is conducted. Commission forensic medical examinations are conducted only in forensic medical examination bureaux. Conducting them in district, inter-district or city units is not permitted. The commission of experts consists of not fewer than three persons. If necessary, clinical specialists are also included.

The role of clinical specialists. In addition to state forensic medical experts, if necessary, clinical specialists of various profiles may be included in the commission. The body that ordered the examination may, at its discretion, determine the composition of the commission or include a particular specialist. If special knowledge is insufficient, the head of the bureau may recommend the inclusion of specialists from other institutions. Thus, when necessary according to the circumstances of the case, a clinical specialist is added to the commission.

t: Who may not be included in the commission
n: Who may not be included in the commission. Heads and specialists of the medical institution where the incident occurred may not be included in the commission. Persons interested in the outcome of the case also cannot be members of the commission. This is necessary to ensure objectivity. A challenge to members is considered by the body that ordered the examination in the manner laid down by law.

Lead expert and rapporteur. The lead expert is usually the head of the forensic expert institution or the head of the relevant department; he organises the work and ensures oversight. The rapporteur draws up the plan of execution, communicates with the person who ordered the examination, prepares the materials and drafts the conclusions. Remember: all members of the commission, including the lead expert and the rapporteur, have equal procedural rights and duties.

t: Rights and duties of the commission
n: Rights and duties of the commission. With permission, the commission has the right to familiarise itself with the materials of the criminal or civil case. It also has the right to require that the employee being held liable be questioned with its participation. All medical institutions, for their part, are obliged to give the commission every assistance.

Inpatient examination. In some cases it is necessary to examine a person in an inpatient setting. On the commission's recommendation and the referral of the ordering body, the person may be admitted to hospital. The results of the examination are submitted to the commission.

t: Structure of the conclusion and introductory part
n: Structure of the conclusion and introductory part. The results are drawn up as the experts' conclusion in an approved form, and it has three parts: introduction, examination and findings. The introduction states the date, place, ground, composition of the commission, case, purpose, questions and materials submitted. For the composition of the commission, position, degree, title, length of service and category are noted.

The examination part. This part briefly sets out the substance of the case and all the information needed to substantiate the conclusion. The following are noted: the ground for instituting the case, an extract from the inspection record, the case history, the outpatient card, treatment, consultations and consilium. Extracts are also given from the examination of the corpse, the pathoanatomical record, laboratory data, the clinical-anatomical conference, the service reference and the interrogation records.

Requirements for extracts and findings. All extracts must be set out with an indication of the sheet of the case materials on which they are found. The findings contain answers to the questions, follow from the examination part, and are objective and scientifically substantiated. Findings based on subjective or conjectural data, or that are incomplete, vague or mutually contradictory, may not be drawn up.

Refusal and disagreement of opinions. If it is established that the data are insufficient, the commission must give reasons for declining to resolve certain questions. The commission may also, on its own initiative, address circumstances that matter to the case but on which no question was put. If opinion is unanimous, the conclusion is drawn up and signed jointly. If opinions differ, each gives a separate conclusion.

The conclusion may state the causes of the offence and the conditions that facilitated it, together with recommendations for eliminating and preventing them. The examination materials are kept in the forensic expert institution for the periods laid down by legislation. Remember: the conclusion may not be given to participants in the proceedings without the permission of the ordering body.

t: Rights of the suspect and the accused
n: Rights of the suspect and the accused. Article 179 of the Criminal Procedure Code sets out the rights of suspects, accused persons and defendants. Before the examination begins, they may see the decision, challenge the expert, and submit additional questions and materials. With permission, they may be present at the examination. After the examination they have the right to see the conclusion and to demand an additional or repeat examination.

t: The responsible employee and limits of participation
n: The responsible employee and the limits of participation. In an examination assessing the care provided, these rights belong to the medical worker being held liable. Participants must not interfere with the investigations, but may require explanation of the substance of the methods and results. Participants are not allowed to attend the commission's meeting and the stage at which the findings are drawn up.

Questioning the experts. If the findings are unclear or have a shortcoming that does not require further investigation, members may be questioned by the inquiry officer, investigator or court. Questioning is conducted only on the existing conclusion. Questioning before the conclusion has been submitted is not permitted.

t: Evaluation of the conclusion (Article 187 of the Criminal Procedure Code)
n: Evaluation of the conclusion, according to Article 187 of the Criminal Procedure Code. The conclusion is evaluated together with other evidence from the standpoint of scientific validity and compliance with procedural norms. For the inquiry officer, investigator and court, the conclusion is not evidence with priority force. Disagreement with the conclusion must be reasoned: the reasons for accepting one of the divergent opinions and rejecting the other are stated.

Examination on the materials according to Kharin. An examination on the materials is conducted when it is not possible to examine a corpse, a living person or physical evidence directly. Most often the case history, outpatient card, pathoanatomical autopsy record and the conclusion of the initial examination are studied. The aim is to establish the causes and circumstances of defects in medical care.

t: Kharin: procedure for instituting a case
n: The procedure for instituting a case according to Kharin. A case concerning employees usually arises from a complaint by patients or their relatives, or on the initiative of the institution's administration. Before a criminal case is instituted, a special departmental commission conducts an official inquiry. The commission sends the materials to the prosecutor's office within 3 days at most after the inquiry is completed. After that the examination on the materials is conducted.

Crime and misdemeanour according to Kharin. By degree of social danger, employees' offences are divided into crimes and misdemeanour offences. A crime carries high social danger and gives rise to criminal liability. Misdemeanours are civil, administrative and disciplinary and are not provided for in the criminal code. Adverse outcomes may be associated with criminal offences, medical errors, accidents and iatrogenic harm. Breaches of professional duty include medical errors, accidents, administrative offences, and negligent and intentional crimes.

Types of medical errors according to Kharin. In forensic medical practice, diagnostic, treatment and organisational errors are distinguished, as well as errors in drawing up and completing medical documents. At the root of a medical error lie the imperfection of science and of methods of investigation, a severe or atypical course of disease, and insufficient knowledge and experience of the physician. A medical error contains no elements of carelessness, inattention, frivolity, overconfidence or professional ignorance. A medical error is not a legal category and, as a rule, does not contain the elements of a crime.

Error, accident and iatrogenic harm. An accident is an adverse outcome associated with chance circumstances, which the physician, acting in good faith, could not foresee or prevent. Iatrogenic harm, by contrast, comprises pathological states and diseases caused by the physician's activity or by medicine in general, most often diagnostic or treatment complications. An iatrogenic disease may arise even from successful treatment of the underlying disease, as a "second disease". Iatrogenic harm also arises when the norms of medical ethics and deontology are violated.

Types of legal liability. The legal liability of a physician for a professional offence includes criminal, civil-law, disciplinary, administrative and financial liability. By degree of social danger, employees' offences are divided into crimes and misdemeanours not provided for in the criminal code. Misdemeanours are civil, administrative and disciplinary.

t: Kharin: offences under the health protection law
n: Now an example from Russian legislation. The Russian "Fundamentals of Legislation on the Protection of Citizens' Health" define several kinds of offences by medical workers. Violation of patients' rights is set out in Article 30; unlawful artificial insemination, abortion and sterilisation in Articles 35-37. Compulsion to take part in biomedical research is in Article 43, euthanasia in Article 45, and trade in organs and tissues in Article 47. Unlawful medical activity and quackery are defined in Articles 54 and 57, breach of the physician's oath in Article 60, disclosure of medical confidentiality in Article 61, and improper performance of duties in Article 68.

t: Kharin: crimes against the person (Criminal Code of the Russian Federation)
n: Crimes against the person under the Criminal Code of Russia. If a medical worker causes death by negligence, he is liable under Article 109, Part 2, or, if he causes grievous harm, under Article 118, Part 2. Compulsion to remove organs or tissues is Article 120, infection with a venereal disease is Article 121, and infection with HIV is a crime under Article 122, Part 4. Unlawful abortion, Article 123, failure to render assistance to a patient, Article 124, and leaving in danger, Article 125, also belong to this group.

t: Kharin: crimes against public health (Criminal Code of the Russian Federation)
n: Crimes against public health under the Criminal Code of Russia. Unlawful circulation of narcotic and psychotropic substances is Article 228, theft or extortion is Article 229, and forgery of prescriptions is Article 233. Unlawful circulation of potent or poisonous substances is Article 234; private medical or pharmaceutical practice is Article 235. Violation of sanitary-epidemiological rules is Article 236, concealment of information about danger is Article 237, and provision of services not meeting safety requirements is Article 238. Violation of safety rules when working with microbiological or other biological agents and toxins is defined by Article 248.

t: Kharin: official crimes (Criminal Code of the Russian Federation)
n: Official crimes under the Criminal Code of Russia. Abuse of official powers, Article 285, and exceeding official powers, Article 286, are crimes against the interests of public service. Unlawful participation in entrepreneurial activity is Article 289, and bribery is Article 290. Official forgery, Article 292, and official negligence, Article 293, may also apply to a medical worker.

Medical error and accident. A medical error is a good-faith mistake in the physician's thoughts and actions; it contains no elements of carelessness, inattention, frivolity or professional ignorance. A medical error is not a legal category; at its root lie the imperfection of science and of methods of investigation, an atypical course or insufficient knowledge. An accident, by contrast, is an outcome associated with chance circumstances, which the physician, acting in good faith, could not foresee or prevent.

Forms of negligence. Carelessness is a form of negligence in which the person did not foresee the consequences but should and could have foreseen them. Negligence, for its part, is a form of fault, appearing as overconfidence or carelessness. The forms of fault consist of intent and negligence. Remember: questions of intent or negligence, guilt or innocence do not fall within the competence of experts; they lie within the competence of the court.

t: Kharin: innocent infliction of harm and extreme necessity
n: Innocent infliction of harm and extreme necessity. In innocent infliction of harm, the person did not realise and could not have realised the danger of the act, or did not foresee the consequences; this is Article 28 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation. In extreme necessity, the act is not a crime if the danger could not be eliminated by other means and the limits were not exceeded; this is Article 39 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation. Justified risk applies if a socially useful aim could not be achieved without risk and measures were taken to prevent harm; this is Article 41 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation.

Examination questions according to Kharin. In the examination of defects in medical care, it is asked whether diagnostic measures were carried out in good time and correctly, and whether the clinical diagnosis was made correctly. It is also asked whether the method of treatment was correctly chosen, whether there were indications for interventions, and whether they were technically performed correctly. In addition, it is established whether there is a direct causal link between the intervention and the adverse outcome, and whether the outcome could have been prevented.

A comparison on the composition of the commission. According to the Uzbek source, that is Giyosov, the commission has not fewer than three persons. According to the Russian source, that is Kharin, a commission on materials consists of at least two specialists; one is the lead expert, and the other is entrusted with organisational support. Each member must personally familiarise himself with the materials. An expert whose opinion differs signs only the findings with which he agrees and sets out a dissenting opinion.

Conclusion and key points. In resolving the questions of a commission examination, the commission of experts answers only questions within its competence. The conclusion is evaluated in the case together with other evidence and does not have priority force.
